notes.definition: Metals that are more reactive than carbon, or that react with carbon, are extracted from their molten compounds by electrolysis. Aluminium is made by electrolysing a molten mixture of aluminium oxide and cryolite, using carbon as the positive electrode (anode).
explanation: Many metals are extracted by heating their oxides with carbon, which removes the oxygen (reduction). This only works for metals less reactive than carbon. Metals that are more reactive than carbon, such as aluminium, sodium and potassium, cannot be reduced by carbon, and some metals react with carbon to form unwanted compounds. These metals are extracted by electrolysis of their molten compounds instead: the metal ions are attracted to the cathode and gain electrons to form the metal.

Electrolysis is expensive because large amounts of energy are needed. Energy is needed to melt the compound (ionic compounds have high melting points) and to produce the large electric current. This is why electrolysis is only used when cheaper methods, such as reduction with carbon, cannot be used.

Aluminium is extracted from aluminium oxide, Al₂O₃. Aluminium oxide has a very high melting point (over 2000 °C). It is dissolved in molten cryolite, an aluminium compound, to make a mixture that melts at about 950 °C. Using this mixture as the electrolyte means a lower temperature is needed, which saves a lot of energy and money. The ions in the molten mixture are free to move.

In the electrolysis cell, the positive electrodes (anodes) are large blocks of carbon (graphite) and the negative electrode (cathode) is the carbon lining of the steel tank. Aluminium ions, Al³⁺, are attracted to the cathode, where they gain electrons and form molten aluminium, which sinks to the bottom and is tapped off. Oxide ions, O²⁻, are attracted to the anodes, where they lose electrons and form oxygen gas. Overall: 2Al₂O₃(l) → 4Al(l) + 3O₂(g).

At the high temperature of the cell, the oxygen produced at the anodes reacts with the carbon to form carbon dioxide: C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g). This means the carbon anodes gradually burn away and must be replaced regularly, which adds to the cost of making aluminium.
keyFacts: Metals more reactive than carbon (or that react with carbon) are extracted by electrolysis.
Electrolysis uses large amounts of energy: to melt the compound and to produce the electric current.
Aluminium is made by electrolysis of aluminium oxide, Al₂O₃.
Aluminium oxide is dissolved in molten cryolite to lower the operating temperature (to about 950 °C).
Both electrodes are made of carbon (graphite); the positive electrode is the anode.
Aluminium forms at the cathode; oxygen forms at the anode.
The anodes react with oxygen to form carbon dioxide, so they burn away and must be replaced.

keyTerms.definition: Obtaining a metal from its compound, such as an ore or oxide.
An aluminium compound which, when molten, dissolves aluminium oxide and lowers the temperature needed for electrolysis.
The molten mixture of aluminium oxide and cryolite, containing ions that are free to move.
The positive electrode; in aluminium extraction it is made of carbon and is gradually burned away.
The negative electrode; in aluminium extraction it is the carbon lining of the cell, where aluminium forms.
Loss of oxygen, or (Higher) gain of electrons; aluminium ions are reduced at the cathode.

workedExamples.title: Choosing an extraction method
workedExamples.question: Explain whether zinc and potassium should be extracted by reduction with carbon or by electrolysis.
steps: Compare each metal with carbon in the reactivity series.
Zinc is less reactive than carbon, so carbon can remove the oxygen from zinc oxide: reduction with carbon (cheaper).
Potassium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot reduce its compounds.
Potassium must be extracted by electrolysis of a molten compound.
workedExamples.answer: Zinc: reduction with carbon. Potassium: electrolysis.

workedExamples.title: Explaining why anodes are replaced
workedExamples.question: Explain why the positive electrodes in aluminium extraction must be replaced regularly.
steps: Oxide ions are discharged at the positive electrode, forming oxygen.
The positive electrodes are made of carbon.
At the high temperature, the oxygen reacts with the carbon: C + O₂ → CO₂.
So the carbon anodes are gradually used up and need replacing.
workedExamples.answer: The oxygen formed reacts with the hot carbon anodes to make carbon dioxide, so the anodes wear away.

workedExamples.title: Higher: balancing the electrons
workedExamples.question: Use the half equations Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al and 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻ to show how many aluminium atoms form for every three oxygen molecules.
steps: Each Al³⁺ needs 3 electrons, so 12 electrons make 12 ÷ 3 = 4 Al atoms.
workedExamples.answer: 4 aluminium atoms for every 3 oxygen molecules.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think cryolite is the ore that aluminium is extracted from.
misconceptions.right: In fact aluminium comes from aluminium oxide. Cryolite is used to dissolve the aluminium oxide and lower the melting temperature.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the cathodes burn away.
misconceptions.right: In fact it is the positive carbon anodes that burn away, because oxygen forms there and reacts with the carbon.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think aluminium is extracted by electrolysis because it is unreactive.
misconceptions.right: In fact aluminium is too reactive to be reduced by carbon, so electrolysis is needed.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think cryolite is a catalyst that speeds up the electrolysis.
misconceptions.right: In fact cryolite lowers the temperature needed to make a molten electrolyte, which reduces energy costs.

realWorld: Aluminium smelters are often built near hydroelectric power stations because the process needs huge amounts of cheap electricity.
Aluminium is used for drinks cans, aircraft and overhead power cables because it is light, strong and resists corrosion.
Sodium and potassium are produced industrially by the electrolysis of their molten chlorides.

For 'why replace the anodes', you must mention oxygen reacting with carbon to form carbon dioxide.
Name the two energy demands: melting the compound and producing the electric current.
Link the choice of method to the reactivity series: above carbon means electrolysis.
Do not confuse the anode (positive, burns away) with the cathode (negative, where aluminium forms).
summary: Metals more reactive than carbon are extracted by electrolysis of molten compounds.
Electrolysis is expensive: energy to melt compounds and make the current.
Aluminium oxide is dissolved in molten cryolite to lower the temperature needed.
Aluminium forms at the cathode and oxygen at the carbon anodes.
Oxygen reacts with the carbon anodes to make CO₂, so anodes must be replaced.

questions.explanation: The anodes are large carbon blocks. Steel is the outer case, and cryolite is part of the electrolyte.

questions.question: Which compound is electrolysed to extract aluminium?
markScheme: 1 mark: aluminium oxide
questions.explanation: Aluminium is extracted from aluminium oxide, Al₂O₃, dissolved in molten cryolite. The cryolite is only there to lower the temperature needed.

questions.question: Why is aluminium oxide mixed with cryolite in the electrolysis cell?
options: Cryolite reacts with oxygen to protect the anodes
Cryolite is a catalyst that speeds up the reaction
The mixture melts at a lower temperature, so less energy is needed
markScheme: 1 mark: lowers the melting point / temperature needed, reducing energy use
questions.explanation: Aluminium oxide melts above 2000 °C. Dissolving it in molten cryolite gives an electrolyte that is molten at about 950 °C, saving energy. Cryolite is not a catalyst.

questions.question: Why do the positive electrodes need to be replaced regularly during aluminium extraction?
options: Aluminium coats them and stops the current
Oxygen reacts with the carbon to form carbon dioxide
They are reduced to carbon monoxide by aluminium
markScheme: 1 mark: oxygen reacts with carbon to form carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Oxygen is produced at the anodes, and at about 950 °C it reacts with the carbon, so the anodes burn away. Aluminium forms at the cathode, not the anode.

questions.explanation: Positive Al³⁺ ions are attracted to the negative electrode and form aluminium. Oxygen (and some carbon dioxide) forms at the positive electrodes.

questions.question: Why is extracting a metal by electrolysis expensive?
options: The metals produced are always impure
The electrodes are made of precious metals
Large amounts of energy are needed to melt the compound and produce the current
The reaction is very slow at high temperatures
markScheme: 1 mark: large amounts of energy to melt the compound and produce the current
questions.explanation: Ionic compounds have high melting points, so heating them takes a lot of energy, and a large electric current is also needed. Carbon electrodes are cheap, not precious metals.

questions.question: Which half equation shows the reaction at the cathode during aluminium extraction?
markScheme: 1 mark: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al
questions.explanation: Each aluminium ion gains three electrons at the cathode (reduction). Al → Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ is the reverse (oxidation), Al³⁺ → Al + 3e⁻ does not balance charge, and 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻ is the anode reaction.

questions.question: Which half equation shows the reaction at the anode during aluminium extraction?
markScheme: 1 mark: 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻
questions.explanation: Two oxide ions each lose two electrons, forming one O₂ molecule and releasing four electrons. Oxygen is diatomic, so O is wrong, and the electrons must appear on the right because they are lost.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows part of the reactivity series.
Which of these metals must be extracted from its compounds by electrolysis?
markScheme: 1 mark: lithium
questions.explanation: Lithium is more reactive than carbon, so it cannot be extracted by heating with carbon. Iron, zinc and copper are less reactive than carbon and can be extracted by reduction with carbon.

questions.question: Apart from oxygen, which gas is given off at the anodes during aluminium extraction?
markScheme: 1 mark: carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: The hot oxygen reacts with the carbon anodes to make carbon dioxide. There are no hydrogen or chloride ions in the electrolyte.

markScheme: 1 mark: oxygen (allow carbon dioxide as a second product, but oxygen is required)

questions.question: Give two reasons why large amounts of energy are used when metals are extracted by electrolysis.
markScheme: 1 mark: to melt the compound (ionic compounds have high melting points)
1 mark: to produce the (large) electric current
questions.explanation: These two energy costs make electrolysis more expensive than reduction with carbon.

markScheme: 1 mark: oxygen is produced at the positive electrode (anode)
1 mark: the anode is made of carbon
1 mark: the oxygen reacts with the carbon (at the high temperature) to form carbon dioxide, so the anode is used up
questions.explanation: The anodes burn away in the oxygen produced on them: C + O₂ → CO₂. This is an ongoing cost of the process.

questions.question: Explain why aluminium cannot be extracted by heating aluminium oxide with carbon.
acceptedAnswers: carbon cannot remove oxygen from aluminium oxide
markScheme: 1 mark: aluminium is more reactive than carbon
1 mark: so carbon cannot reduce aluminium oxide / remove the oxygen
questions.explanation: Carbon can only displace less reactive metals from their oxides. Aluminium holds on to oxygen more strongly than carbon does.

questions.question: Explain why the aluminium oxide must be molten (or dissolved in molten cryolite) for electrolysis.
markScheme: 1 mark: in the solid the ions are fixed in the lattice
1 mark: when molten / dissolved the ions are free to move to the electrodes and carry the current
questions.explanation: Electrolysis only works if Al³⁺ and O²⁻ ions can move to the electrodes.

questions.question:
In the extraction of aluminium, the carbon positive electrodes wear away.
Write a balanced symbol equation for the reaction that causes this.
Include state symbols.
markScheme: 1 mark: C + O₂ → CO₂
1 mark: correct state symbols (s), (g), (g)
questions.explanation: Carbon (solid) reacts with oxygen gas to make carbon dioxide gas. This is a combustion reaction at the high temperature of the cell.

questions.question: Write a balanced symbol equation for the overall decomposition of aluminium oxide during electrolysis.
markScheme: 1 mark: correct formulae Al₂O₃ → Al + O₂
1 mark: correctly balanced: 2Al₂O₃ → 4Al + 3O₂
questions.explanation: Oxygen appears as 3 atoms in Al₂O₃ and 2 in O₂. The lowest common multiple is 6, giving 2Al₂O₃ and 3O₂, then 4Al balances the aluminium.

questions.question:
Aluminium is extracted by electrolysis.
Aluminium extraction plants are often built near hydroelectric power stations.
Suggest why.
markScheme: 1 mark: electrolysis needs a very large amount of electricity (energy)
1 mark: hydroelectric power provides a cheap / reliable supply, reducing costs
questions.explanation: Electricity is one of the biggest costs of aluminium extraction, so a cheap, nearby source makes the process more economical.

questions.question:
Aluminium is extracted by the electrolysis of aluminium oxide.
Explain why this electrolysis is a redox reaction.
Refer to the ions at each electrode in your answer.
acceptedAnswers: both happen at the same time
markScheme: 1 mark: aluminium ions gain electrons at the cathode, so they are reduced
1 mark: oxide ions lose electrons at the anode, so they are oxidised
1 mark: reduction and oxidation happen at the same time, so it is a redox reaction
questions.explanation: Reduction is gain of electrons and oxidation is loss of electrons (OIL RIG). Both processes occur together in the cell.

questions.question: Name one metal, other than aluminium, that is extracted by electrolysis.
markScheme: 1 mark: any metal more reactive than carbon, for example sodium, potassium, lithium or calcium
questions.explanation: Any metal above carbon in the reactivity series must be extracted by electrolysis of a molten compound.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a cell used to extract aluminium from aluminium oxide.
Describe and explain how aluminium is extracted from aluminium oxide by electrolysis.
In your answer you should refer to:
• the electrolyte
• the electrodes
• the products
• the costs of the process.

markScheme: Indicative content: aluminium is more reactive than carbon so cannot be extracted by reduction with carbon; aluminium oxide is dissolved in molten cryolite; this lowers the melting point (to about 950 °C) so less energy is needed; ions are free to move in the molten electrolyte; electrodes are carbon (graphite); cathode is negative (carbon lining), anode is positive (carbon blocks); Al³⁺ ions attracted to the cathode, gain electrons, form molten aluminium which sinks and is tapped off; O²⁻ ions attracted to the anode, lose electrons, form oxygen; oxygen reacts with the hot carbon anodes to form carbon dioxide so the anodes must be replaced; large amounts of energy needed to melt the electrolyte and produce the current, so the process is expensive.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): detailed, well-organised description and explanation covering cryolite and why it is used, both electrode products, why anodes are replaced, and energy costs.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes the process with correct products and at least one explanation (for example cryolite lowers the melting point, or anodes burn away).
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple relevant statements such as aluminium forms at the cathode or electricity is used.
0 marks: nothing worthy of credit.
questions.explanation: The strongest answers explain each feature: why electrolysis (reactivity), why cryolite (lower temperature, less energy), what forms where (aluminium at the cathode, oxygen at the anode) and why the anodes are replaced (they react to form CO₂).

questions.question:
The extraction of aluminium uses a lot of energy and is expensive.
Explain why the costs are high.
Explain how using cryolite helps to reduce the costs.
markScheme: Indicative content: energy needed to melt the ionic compound (aluminium oxide melts above 2000 °C); energy needed to produce the large electric current; carbon anodes react with oxygen to form carbon dioxide and must be regularly replaced, adding cost; cryolite dissolves aluminium oxide to form a mixture that is molten at about 950 °C; lower temperature means less energy is needed to keep the electrolyte molten, so costs are reduced.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): explains at least two sources of cost and clearly explains how cryolite reduces the energy needed.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): identifies a cost, or states that cryolite lowers the melting point, with limited explanation.
0 marks: nothing worthy of credit.
questions.explanation: There are three cost factors: heating to melt the electrolyte, electricity for the current, and replacing the anodes. Cryolite tackles the first by lowering the temperature needed.

questions.question: How are metals that are more reactive than carbon extracted from their compounds?
markScheme: 1 mark: electrolysis of a molten compound
questions.explanation: Carbon cannot reduce compounds of metals more reactive than itself, and iron is even less reactive, so electrolysis is needed.
